transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I came in because, well, it's just been so hard lately. You see, I've been in sales for over thirty years—services, mostly, business-to-business stuff—and my whole life, my whole career, has been about talking to people, connecting, you know? I used to be the guy who could walk into a room, strike up a conversation with anyone, and just... enjoy the day. But lately, most days, I wake up and there's just this... this heavy, hollow feeling right here in my chest. It's like... it's like the old Ruben is just gone. Completely gone. I lie there in the morning, and the alarm goes off, and instead of thinking about the accounts I need to call or the people I'm going to see, I just feel this crushing weight. It's not just a bad mood, it's this deep, empty sensation that just sits there, day in and day out. I try to shake it off, I really do, but it's like I'm a completely different person now, and I just don't know where the guy who used to love his life went.
How long have you been feeling this heavy, hollow sensation?

Well, it's... it's been about eight months now. Eight months of waking up every single day with that exact feeling. I can actually trace it back, you know, right to the time when... when the new regional manager came on board. He's this young guy, probably half my age, and he just... he started coming down on me, really hard. And not just that, he started taking away my accounts. Accounts I've handled for years! I mean, I built relationships with these people, I knew their kids' names, their anniversaries... and he just reassigned them like it was nothing. Just shuffled the paperwork and handed them off to some junior reps who don't know the first thing about our clients' businesses. That was right around eight months ago, maybe early spring, and ever since then, it's just been this... this steady slide downward. Every morning I wake up and I think about those accounts, about how I used to be the top producer, and now... now I'm just sitting here, feeling like I've been completely hollowed out. Eight months of this, doctor. Every single day.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, no... no, I don't. And that's the thing that really scares my wife, honestly. We used to be so active, you know? I mean, I'm 58, but I've always had energy to burn. We had this whole routine. Tuesday nights were for my bowling league—I've been in that league for fifteen years, doctor, fifteen years! And I loved it, the camaraderie, the noise, the awful pizza. And on the weekends, I'd be out in the garden for hours, getting my hands dirty, growing these incredible heirloom tomatoes. My wife, she loves art, so we'd go to gallery shows downtown, or we'd go out dancing. We used to love dancing. But now... now I just... I don't care about any of it. The bowling ball has been sitting in the hall closet for months. The garden is just weeds right now, I haven't even gone out there to look at it. When my wife asks if I want to go to a show or out for a spin on the dance floor, I just... I sit there in my armchair and I make up excuses. I tell her my back hurts, or I'm too tired from work—even though I'm barely doing anything at work these days. I just sit there because the thought of getting up, of putting on nice clothes, of having to smile and pretend I'm having a good time... it just doesn't feel worth the effort anymore. None of it does. It's like the color has just been drained out of everything I used to love.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

Guilt... yeah. Yeah, I do. All the time, doctor. I sit in that armchair I told you about, and my mind just spins and spins. I keep telling myself I'm completely useless now. Just... useless. I mean, I think about all those years, over thirty years of working my tail off, taking care of my clients, making sure they had exactly what they needed, when they needed it. And providing for my family, too. My wife and I, we built a good life. We put our kids through school, we paid off the mortgage early... I was the provider. I was the guy who got things done. But now? Now I look at myself and I think, what was it all for? It feels like none of those years even count anymore, you know? Because I can't even handle this job. I can't handle some kid fresh out of business school taking my accounts, and I can't even muster the strength to fight back or prove him wrong. I just let it happen. And I feel so incredibly guilty about that. I look at my wife, and she's trying so hard to be supportive, bringing me coffee, asking if I want to talk, and I just feel like this massive burden on her. I blame myself for not being stronger, for letting this new manager break me down so easily. A real man, a real professional, wouldn't just crumble like this, right? But here I am, unable to even go out and bowl a few frames, let alone be the husband and the provider I'm supposed to be. It's just this constant loop in my head, doctor, telling me I've failed, that I'm just... I'm just washed up and worthless.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead?

Well... I... I don't know if I'd say I've made a plan or anything like that, but... but the thoughts are there. They're definitely there, doctor. It's like I was saying about sitting in that armchair, right? I sit there for hours, just watching the dust motes in the sunlight, and my mind goes to these really dark places. Darker than I ever thought possible for me. I look at my wife—she's so good, you know, she really is—and I think about my kids, my two boys who are grown and have their own lives now. And I start thinking... I start thinking that maybe, just maybe, they would all be better off if I just... didn't wake up tomorrow. 

I mean, look at me. I'm not providing anymore, I'm not the man they always looked up to. I'm just this heavy weight pulling everyone down. I think about my life insurance policy, how it's fully paid up, and how my wife wouldn't have to worry about money or... or worry about taking care of a husband who can't even get off the couch to go to a bowling alley. It just seems like it would be easier for them. A clean break. 

And honestly, doctor... those thoughts, they terrify me. They really do. Because I've always been a fighter. I've always been the guy who pushes through, who closes the deal, who fixes the leaky faucet and keeps everything running. But now? Now I have these thoughts creeping in, whispering that it would just be better to let go, to just slip away in the night. And it scares me because... because I don't trust myself anymore. I don't trust my own mind. I used to know exactly who I was and what I would do in any situation, but now, when I'm sitting there in the quiet of the house, and that thought pops into my head... I just don't know. I don't trust myself the way I used to, and that's... that's a really hard thing for a man my age to admit.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

Like I was touching on just a few minutes ago, doctor... no. There really isn't. Not a single thing. I know it probably sounds extreme to hear someone say they don't enjoy anything at all, but it's the honest truth. 

I sit there in that armchair I told you about, and sometimes I actually try to force myself to think of something, anything, that might bring a little bit of that old spark back. I'll look over toward the hall closet where my bowling ball is, or I'll see my wife looking at the arts and entertainment section in the Sunday paper, and I try to muster up even a fraction of the excitement I used to feel for those gallery shows or our nights out dancing. We used to be such good dancers, you know? People would actually stop and watch us sometimes when the band played a good swing number. We had this whole routine. 

But now... I just look at her reading that paper and I feel completely empty. I don't want to go to the gallery, I don't want to step foot on a dance floor, I don't want to go anywhere near my garden... I mean, the tomatoes are probably completely choked out by weeds and dead by now anyway, which is a shame, a real shame, because I used to take such pride in them. But I just sit there and I make up those excuses I mentioned earlier. I'll say my back is acting up, or my knees are stiff, or I'm just too drained from the office... whatever I can think of to just stay put in that chair. Because honestly, doctor, when I really think about getting up and doing any of those things I used to look forward to so much... it just feels like climbing a mountain. None of it feels worth the effort anymore. Not one single thing.
Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?

Moving slower? I... I don't really think so. Not exactly. I mean, I'm not moving much at all, really. Like I've been saying, I just sit in that armchair for most of the day. But when I do actually get up to, say, go to the bathroom or get a glass of water from the kitchen, I don't feel like my legs are moving in slow motion or anything like that. 

And my wife hasn't said anything about me talking slower, either. Which is something I think she would notice, because in my line of work—sales, you know, selling services for over thirty years—you have to be quick on your feet. You have to talk fast, think fast, anticipate what the client is going to say before they even finish their sentence. Over all those years of doing that, you build up a certain rhythm. A certain cadence to how you speak. You learn how to read the room and match the pace of the person across the desk from you. If they're a fast talker, you speed up. If they're methodical, you slow down a beat to make them comfortable. But my natural state was always... energetic. Hustling. Always moving onto the next pitch, the next account. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm moving or speaking slower in a physical sense. It's more just... I'm not doing much of anything. The engine is just turned off completely. I'm not out there pacing the living room floor while on a conference call, or rushing out the front door with my briefcase half-open because I'm running five minutes behind for a breakfast meeting. I'm just planted in that chair by the window. So maybe it looks to my wife like I'm slower just because I'm... well, stationary. But the actual physical movement, the actual speed of the words coming out of my mouth when I do speak... no, I haven't really noticed a change in the speed of it. Just the frequency, I guess you could say. Because, honestly, why talk when there's nothing worthwhile left to say, right?
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past few months?

Weight? No, no, I wouldn't say I've lost weight. Actually, it might be the opposite, if I'm being perfectly honest with you, doctor. I haven't stepped on a scale in... well, it has to be months. We have this old mechanical scale in the master bathroom, the kind with the little dial that spins, you know? My wife bought it years ago at a department store that isn't even in business anymore. But I just walk right past it these days. 

I mean, considering how I just sit in that armchair all day, I'm certainly not burning any calories. I'm not out there walking the golf course with clients or rushing through airport terminals trying to catch a connecting flight to Chicago or Dallas like I used to. Back then, I was always on the move, always grabbing a quick sandwich at a deli or eating a salad at a business lunch. Now? Now my wife, bless her heart, she still tries to make these nice dinners for us. Pot roast, chicken casseroles, things like that. And I eat them, mostly just because they're put in front of me and I don't want to hurt her feelings. She puts so much effort into it, trying to keep some sense of normalcy in the house, trying to pretend we're still the same couple we were a year ago. 

So I sit there at the dining room table, and I chew the food, and I swallow it, but I don't really taste it. It's just... fuel, I guess. Though fuel for what, I couldn't tell you, since the engine isn't running. But no, to answer your question, my clothes don't feel any looser. If anything, my belt feels a little tighter around the middle from all the sitting. It's funny, isn't it? You'd think being this miserable would eat away at you physically, make you waste away to nothing. But instead, I'm just sitting there, taking up the same amount of space, maybe even a little more, while feeling like there's absolutely nothing left inside. So no, doctor, no weight loss that I've noticed. Just the same heavy guy in the same heavy chair.
Do you still enjoy the company of friends and family?

Company? Well, doctor, it kind of goes right back to what I was telling you earlier about the bowling and the dancing and all that. Because that right there—that *was* my company, you know? That was my social life. 

My wife, obviously, was my partner for the gallery shows and the swing dancing. And the bowling... I've been in a Thursday night league with the same group of guys—Tom, Jimmy, and Mike—for over fifteen years. We used to grab a beer afterward, talk about our accounts, complain about our bosses, just shoot the breeze. I used to really look forward to all of that. I was usually the guy organizing the outings, the one saying, "Hey guys, let's get out to the lanes early," or "Honey, let's go see that new exhibit downtown." 

But now? Now I don't even want to see them. I don't want to see anybody. Just like with working in the garden, I just sit in my chair. When Tom calls about the league, I just stare at the phone and let it go to voicemail. When my wife asks if we should invite our daughter over for a Sunday roast, I just... I make up those excuses I told you about. I'll tell her my stomach is off, or I'm just too exhausted from dealing with clients all week, even though, frankly, I'm barely keeping my head above water at work either. 

Being around people, even the people I love, even my own family... it requires a kind of energy I just don't have anymore. Having to smile, having to keep up a conversation, having to pretend I care about what's going on in their lives when I feel so completely dead inside... it's exhausting just thinking about it. You have to put on a performance, and as a salesman, I know all about putting on a performance, but the tank is completely empty. So, no, I don't enjoy their company anymore. I just avoid them entirely. Because like I said about all those other things I used to love... getting up and actually engaging with anyone just doesn't feel worth the effort. It's just too much.
Do you feel like you're resting or sleeping more than usual?

Resting? Well, I mean, like I was saying, I'm sitting in that armchair by the window all day long, so I guess physically you could say my body is resting. I'm certainly not exerting any energy. But sleeping? God, no. I wish I was sleeping more. It's actually the exact opposite. 

Nighttime is... it's awful, to be honest with you. I go up to bed, and my wife, she usually falls asleep pretty quick, usually within ten or fifteen minutes. She's always been a good sleeper. But me? I just lie there flat on my back. I just stare up at the ceiling. We have this white ceiling fan in the master bedroom, the kind with the little brass pull chains, and the streetlamp from the corner casts this faint shadow across it through the blinds. I just stare at those shadows for hours. 

My body is completely dead, but my mind is just... it's stuck. I lie there replaying work over and over again. Every missed call, every account I'm neglecting, every client I'm letting down because I just can't bring myself to care or make the effort anymore. In my business, you know, you're only as good as your last quarter, and I just keep turning it all over in my head, thinking about how I'm dropping the ball, going over conversations I had or should have had, just spinning my wheels in the dark while the rest of the house is dead silent. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off—usually out of pure exhaustion—it never lasts. I'll snap awake, and I'll look over at the red numbers on the digital clock on the nightstand, and it's always right around three or four in the morning. Every single night. Three-thirty, four-fifteen. And that's it. I'm done sleeping. But the worst part is, I don't wake up feeling refreshed. I wake up already completely worn out, if that makes any sense. Like I just ran a marathon in my sleep. So I just lie there for the next few hours, watching the room slowly get lighter, just absolutely dreading the day. Just dreading the sun coming up, because it means I have to get out of that bed, go downstairs, sit in that chair, and face another day of feeling like this. So, no, I'm definitely not sleeping more. I'm barely sleeping at all.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or having trouble sitting still?

Fidgeting? No, no... honestly, doctor, it's the exact opposite of that. Like I mentioned before, about that armchair in the living room? I just sink into that thing and I don't move. I mean, I really don't move. I could sit there for three, four hours and not even shift my weight. 

My wife actually came in on Tuesday—she had just gotten back from the grocery store, she goes to that big one over on Route 9 because she says they have a much better produce section than the local place—and she told me I was in the exact same position as when she left. And she was gone for at least an hour and a half. I hadn't even turned my head. 

It's strange, really, because back when I was actually functioning, back when I was really hustling and managing my service accounts, I was always a pacer. I'd get on a call with a client, trying to negotiate a contract or smooth over some issue, and I'd be walking all over the house. Pacing the hallway, clicking my pen, tapping my foot under the dining table if I had to sit down. I used to have all this... this drive, you know? This nervous energy to get things done and close the deal. 

But now? That energy is just completely gone. Drained out of me. I don't tap my foot, I don't bounce my leg, I don't wring my hands. I just sit there like a lump, like I'm just another piece of the furniture. My arms just rest on the armrests, and they feel so heavy, like they're made of lead or wet sand or something. Sometimes I just stare at my own hands and I wonder how I used to gesture so much when I talked, because now just the thought of lifting them feels like too much work. So, no, sitting still isn't a problem for me at all. It's about the only thing I do.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your family?

A burden? Yeah. Yeah, I do. More than a burden, really. I just... I keep telling myself I’m completely useless now. And that's a really hard pill to swallow, doctor. It really is. 

Because for my whole life, ever since I got out of high school and started in this business, my entire identity was tied up in being the guy who provided. I was the one out there hustling, driving all over the place, taking care of my clients, making sure they had the services they needed so they'd renew their contracts year after year. I did all of that so I could provide for my family. So we could have a nice life, so my wife could have a nice home, so we could pay for our daughter's things. I prided myself on being reliable. 

But now... now I look at myself, and I can't even handle this job anymore. I can't pick up the phone. I can't close a deal. I'm letting everyone down. And because of that, it feels like... it feels like all those years of taking care of clients and providing for my family just don't count for anything anymore. Like they've just been completely erased. What does it matter that I worked my fingers to the bone for thirty years if I can't even pull my own weight today? 

My wife is picking up all the slack, doing all the shopping, taking care of the house, tip-toeing around me while I just sit there in that chair like a piece of lead. She's making excuses for me to our daughter, probably making excuses to our friends, and I'm just... I'm just dead weight. A total zero. It doesn't matter what kind of provider I was in the past, because right now, today, I am absolutely useless to them. I'm just dragging her down, dragging everyone down with me, and I can't stop thinking about how unfair it is to her to be stuck with a husband who can't even function.
Do you feel like you're moving or speaking more slowly than you used to, or do you have trouble sitting still?

Moving or speaking slower? I... I don't really know, to be honest with you. I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, as far as the sitting still part goes, like I was just saying a minute ago, that's definitely not an issue. I'm practically glued to that armchair in the living room. I don't have any trouble staying in one spot. 

But speaking slower? I just... I don't talk to anyone anymore, doctor, so how would I even know? Back when I was working my territory, I was on the phone eight, maybe ten hours a day. Talking fast, pitching, negotiating, trying to get ahead of the objections before the client even brought them up. You have to be quick on your feet in sales. Now? The phone rings—it's probably a client wondering where their service renewal contract is, or my manager wondering why my numbers are in the toilet—and I just watch the screen light up. I just watch it ring until it goes to voicemail. 

The only person I really talk to these days is my wife, and even then, it's just a few words here and there. She'll come in and ask if I want a turkey sandwich for lunch, and I just say no. She asks how I'm doing, I say fine. There's not really enough conversation happening for me to tell you if the words are coming out slower than they used to. I'm just not saying much of anything. 

And moving? Well, since I'm just sitting in that chair all day, I'm not really moving enough to gauge the speed of it, you know? When I do finally force myself to get up to go to the bathroom, or when I go up the stairs to bed to lie awake all night under that ceiling fan, I guess I just walk like normal? I haven't really paid attention to it. I just know I don't want to move at all. The desire is gone. So, I can't really say I've noticed being slower, just... just stopped, I guess. Everything's just stopped.
Do you feel like you have a lot of restless energy and can't sit still?

I... doctor, didn't you just ask me that? Or maybe I'm losing my mind along with everything else. But no, like I was just saying a minute ago, I don't have any trouble sitting still. And I definitely don't have any energy, restless or otherwise. 

I mean, I really wish I did have some kind of restless energy, because maybe then I'd actually get up and do something useful around the house. Maybe I'd go out to the garage and finally sort through those boxes of old client files I brought home back in, what was it, 2018? My wife's been asking me to break those down for recycling for years. But I don't. I just sit in that same chair in the living room. There's no bouncing my leg, no pacing the floor, no urge to get up and move. Nothing. 

It's actually kind of funny, in a really pathetic sort of way, because back when I was really hitting my numbers, my old regional manager used to tell me I was like a shark. You know, how they say a shark has to keep swimming or it dies? That was me. Always driving to the next appointment, always moving, always onto the next thing. But now... it's like someone just pulled the plug. I'm just a stone. A heavy rock sitting at the bottom of a pond, just watching the water go by. There's no restlessness at all. Just this heavy, awful stillness. I really don't know how else to explain it to you, but no, I'm not restless. I just don't move.
Do you feel like you're unable to initiate or complete tasks due to a lack of energy or motivation?

Energy or motivation? I... I really couldn't tell you if that's what it is. I mean, I'm not sure if I'd use those words, because I don't even know what motivation feels like anymore to know if I'm missing it, if that makes sense. And as for energy, well, like I said before, I'm just sitting in a chair all day. It's not like I'm physically exhausted from running a marathon or out knocking on doors for twelve hours like I used to. I haven't done anything to be tired from. So I don't know if it's a lack of energy, exactly. I just... I just don't start things. 

Take the lawn, for example. We live on this corner lot, about a half-acre, and I've always taken a lot of pride in it. For thirty years, I was out there every Saturday morning by eight o'clock, edging the driveway, making sure the mulch was fresh around the oak trees, keeping the lines perfectly straight. The neighbors used to joke that I loved that grass more than my car. But over the last few weeks, the grass just kept getting higher and higher. It was practically up to my shins. 

Last weekend, my wife—bless her heart, she's already doing so much—she finally just went out to the shed and dragged the mower out herself. I was sitting right there in my chair, looking out the front window, and I watched her do it. It's an older gas model, a Toro, and you have to really give the pull cord a good, hard yank and prime it just right or it floods. I watched her struggling with it, pulling and pulling, and I knew exactly what she was doing wrong. I knew I should just walk out the front door and take over. I knew it was my job as the husband, as the man of the house, to do it. 

But I just sat there. I didn't feel tired. I didn't feel physically weak. I just stared through the glass, and it felt like there was this invisible, hundred-foot-thick concrete wall between me and that front door. I just couldn't make myself stand up and walk outside. Is that a lack of motivation, doctor? I really don't know. I don't know what the right word for it is. I just felt completely empty. 

And it's like that with everything now. The mail comes in, and my wife puts the bills in this neat little stack on the kitchen counter. I used to pay them the exact day they arrived, wrote the check, put the stamp on, done. Now I walk past the kitchen, I look at the stack, and I just turn away and go back to my chair. I don't feel sleepy when I look at the mail. I just... don't do it. So I can't really tell you if I'm unable to initiate these things because of my energy levels. I really don't know the reason. I just know that nothing is getting done, and I don't know how to fix it.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slower than they used to?

Slower? I... well, I don't really think so. Or at least, I haven't noticed them being slower. It's more like... well, to know if a car is driving slow, it actually has to be moving down the road, right? My mind right now, it's not really driving down the road at all. It's just parked. 

Back when I was working my territory, my brain was like a steel trap. I had to remember client names, their spouses' names, what their kids were studying in college, exactly what quarter their fiscal budget opened up so I could time my calls perfectly. I was always thinking three steps ahead of the person on the other end of the line. I was sharp. Now? I sit in that brown leather armchair I told you about, and I just stare out the window. Like yesterday, I sat there and watched the mail carrier walk up the entire block. He stopped at the Henderson's, stopped at the Miller's, came up our front walk... and I didn't have a single thought about any of it. I wasn't wondering if he was bringing a check or a bill. My head was just completely blank. 

It's just empty space now. So if my wife comes into the room and asks me a question, it's not that my brain is taking a long time to process her words, or that I'm thinking in slow motion. I just don't have anything to say because there's nothing going on up there. I don't care enough to form a thought about whatever it is she's asking. I just draw a blank. So I wouldn't say my thoughts are slower, doctor. I really wouldn't. They're just... just not there. There's really nothing going on in my head for most of the day, just a lot of quiet.
Do you find it difficult to make decisions?

Decisions? No, I... I wouldn't say it's difficult. I mean, to have a hard time making a decision, you have to actually care about the outcome, right? You have to weigh the options and worry about making the wrong choice. I just don't have any of that going on. 

It's funny, because in my line of work—well, my old line of work, I guess—decisions were my bread and butter. When you're selling commercial service contracts, you're making a hundred little judgment calls a minute. You walk into a prospect's office, you look at the photos on their desk, you read their body language, and you instantly decide how to pitch them. Do you talk about golf? Do you keep it strictly numbers? Do you push the premium tier right out of the gate or just get your foot in the door with the basic package? I never hesitated. I was decisive. I'd make the call, close the deal, and boom, onto the next one. 

But now... it's not like I'm sitting here agonizing over things. It's just that there aren't any decisions to make. Or if there are, I just leave them to my wife because it doesn't matter to me either way. Like, she'll come in around five o'clock and ask if I want chicken or pork chops for dinner. A person who has trouble making decisions might sit there and hum and haw, trying to figure out what they have a taste for, getting stressed out about picking the right one. But me? I just say, "Whatever you want." And it's not because I'm stuck between the two. It's because I genuinely do not care. I don't care if it's chicken, I don't care if it's pork, I don't care if it's a bowl of dry cereal. 

There's no struggle. I wake up, I move to the living room, and I sit. I don't debate what channel to put the TV on because I don't turn the TV on. I don't decide what shirt to wear because I just pull on whatever is sitting right there on top of the laundry basket. So, no, doctor, I'm not having any trouble making decisions. I just don't have any preference about anything in the world anymore, so there's really nothing to decide. It's all just exactly the same to me.
Do you feel your condition is worsening over time?

Worsening? I... I don't know if I'd say it's getting worse, exactly. It's more like... well, it's just been this same flat line for a while now. I mean, when you hit the bottom, you can't really fall any further, right? 

I think back to when this first started, maybe a couple of months ago. I was still trying to keep up appearances, you know? I'd still put on a decent shirt, maybe try to read the paper in the morning, even if none of the words were sinking in. I remember one Tuesday, I actually drove out to the hardware store to get some new sprinkler heads because a couple of ours had cracked over the winter. I walked the aisles, picked out the parts, paid the cashier. I felt completely hollow doing it, like I was just going through the motions in a play, but I was still doing it. 

But now? Now I wouldn't even think about getting in the car. I wouldn't even care if every sprinkler head in the yard was busted. But is that getting worse? Or is it just that I finally stopped pretending? I don't really know. 

It feels like I've just settled into this... this heavy, gray routine. I wake up, I sit in the chair, I watch the dust motes float in the sunlight coming through the front window, and I wait for the day to end. And the next day is exactly the same. And the day after that. There aren't any new symptoms cropping up. I'm not suddenly feeling a different kind of terrible. It's just the exact same nothingness, day in and day out. 

My wife, she keeps track of the days. She'll say, "Frank, you haven't been out of the house since last Thursday," or "Frank, you've been wearing those same sweatpants for three days." And I hear her, and I know she's right, but it doesn't feel like a progression to me. It doesn't feel like a disease that's spreading or a storm that's getting stronger. It just feels like a clock that stopped ticking. The hands are stuck at the exact same time they were stuck at yesterday, and they'll probably be stuck there tomorrow. So I really couldn't tell you if it's worsening, doctor. I just don't know how to measure it when everything is just so completely still.
Do you feel like you're restless or have an inability to sit still?

Restless? I... no, not at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. I think I mentioned that brown leather armchair in the living room earlier, the one by the front window? And moving? Well, since I'm just sitting in that chair all day, I'm not really moving enough to gauge the speed of it, you know? When I do finally force myself to get up to go to the bathroom, or when I go up the stairs to bed to lie awake all night under that ceiling fan, I guess I just walk like normal? I haven't really paid attention to it. I just know I don't want to move at all. The desire is gone. So, I can't really say I've noticed being slower, just... just stopped, I guess. Everything's just stopped.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have a lot of restless energy and can't sit still?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation (restless energy, inability to sit still), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I... doctor, didn't you just ask me that? Or maybe I'm losing my mind along with everything else. But no, like I was just saying a minute ago, I don't have any trouble sitting still. And I definitely don't have any energy, restless or otherwise. 

I mean, I really wish I did have some kind of restless energy, because maybe then I'd actually get up and do something useful around the house. Maybe I'd go out to the garage and finally sort through those boxes of old client files I brought home back in, what was it, 2018? My wife's been asking me to break those down for recycling for years. But I don't. I just sit in that same chair in the living room. There's no bouncing my leg, no pacing the floor, no urge to get up and move. Nothing. 

It's actually kind of funny, in a really pathetic sort of way, because back when I was really hitting my numbers, my old regional manager used to tell me I was like a shark. You know, how they say a shark has to keep swimming or it dies? That was me. Always driving to the next appointment, always moving, always onto the next thing. But now... it's like someone just pulled the plug. I'm just a stone. A heavy rock sitting at the bottom of a pond, just watching the water go by. There's no restlessness at all. Just this heavy, awful stillness. I really don't know how else to explain it to you, but no, I'm not restless. I just don't move.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to initiate or complete tasks due to a lack of energy or motivation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue, loss of energy, or lack of motivation to complete tasks, which corresponds to the symptom of Fatigue/Loss of Energy. This is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energy or motivation? I... I really couldn't tell you if that's what it is. I mean, I'm not sure if I'd use those words, because I don't even know what motivation feels like anymore to know if I'm missing it, if that makes sense. And as for energy, well, like I said before, I'm just sitting in a chair all day. It's not like I'm physically exhausted from running a marathon or out knocking on doors for twelve hours like I used to. I haven't done anything to be tired from. So I don't know if it's a lack of energy, exactly. I just... I just don't start things. 

Take the lawn, for example. We live on this corner lot, about a half-acre, and I've always taken a lot of pride in it. For thirty years, I was out there every Saturday morning by eight o'clock, edging the driveway, making sure the mulch was fresh around the oak trees, keeping the lines perfectly straight. The neighbors used to joke that I loved that grass more than my car. But over the last few weeks, the grass just kept getting higher and higher. It was practically up to my shins. 

Last weekend, my wife—bless her heart, she's already doing so much—she finally just went out to the shed and dragged the mower out herself. I was sitting right there in my chair, looking out the front window, and I watched her do it. It's an older gas model, a Toro, and you have to really give the pull cord a good, hard yank and prime it just right or it floods. I watched her struggling with it, pulling and pulling, and I knew exactly what she was doing wrong. I knew I should just walk out the front door and take over. I knew it was my job as the husband, as the man of the house, to do it. 

But I just sat there. I didn't feel tired. I didn't feel physically weak. I just stared through the glass, and it felt like there was this invisible, hundred-foot-thick concrete wall between me and that front door. I just couldn't make myself stand up and walk outside. Is that a lack of motivation, doctor? I really don't know. I don't know what the right word for it is. I just felt completely empty. 

And it's like that with everything now. The mail comes in, and my wife puts the bills in this neat little stack on the kitchen counter. I used to pay them the exact day they arrived, wrote the check, put the stamp on, done. Now I walk past the kitchen, I look at the stack, and I just turn away and go back to my chair. I don't feel sleepy when I look at the mail. I just... don't do it. So I can't really tell you if I'm unable to initiate these things because of my energy levels. I really don't know the reason. I just know that nothing is getting done, and I don't know how to fix it.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slower than they used to?

patient.answer:
Slower? I... well, I don't really think so. Or at least, I haven't noticed them being slower. It's more like... well, to know if a car is driving slow, it actually has to be moving down the road, right? My mind right now, it's not really driving down the road at all. It's just parked. 

Back when I was working my territory, my brain was like a steel trap. I had to remember client names, their spouses' names, what their kids were studying in college, exactly what quarter their fiscal budget opened up so I could time my calls perfectly. I was always thinking three steps ahead of the person on the other end of the line. I was sharp. Now? I sit in that brown leather armchair I told you about, and I just stare out the window. Like yesterday, I sat there and watched the mail carrier walk up the entire block. He stopped at the Henderson's, stopped at the Miller's, came up our front walk... and I didn't have a single thought about any of it. I wasn't wondering if he was bringing a check or a bill. My head was just completely blank. 

It's just empty space now. So if my wife comes into the room and asks me a question, it's not that my brain is taking a long time to process her words, or that I'm thinking in slow motion. I just don't have anything to say because there's nothing going on up there. I don't care enough to form a thought about whatever it is she's asking. I just draw a blank. So I wouldn't say my thoughts are slower, doctor. I really wouldn't. They're just... just not there. There's really nothing going on in my head for most of the day, just a lot of quiet.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you find it difficult to make decisions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty making decisions (indecisiveness), which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Decisions? No, I... I wouldn't say it's difficult. I mean, to have a hard time making a decision, you have to actually care about the outcome, right? You have to weigh the options and worry about making the wrong choice. I just don't have any of that going on. 

It's funny, because in my line of work—well, my old line of work, I guess—decisions were my bread and butter. When you're selling commercial service contracts, you're making a hundred little judgment calls a minute. You walk into a prospect's office, you look at the photos on their desk, you read their body language, and you instantly decide how to pitch them. Do you talk about golf? Do you keep it strictly numbers? Do you push the premium tier right out of the gate or just get your foot in the door with the basic package? I never hesitated. I was decisive. I'd make the call, close the deal, and boom, onto the next one. 

But now... it's not like I'm sitting here agonizing over things. It's just that there aren't any decisions to make. Or if there are, I just leave them to my wife because it doesn't matter to me either way. Like, she'll come in around five o'clock and ask if I want chicken or pork chops for dinner. A person who has trouble making decisions might sit there and hum and haw, trying to figure out what they have a taste for, getting stressed out about picking the right one. But me? I just say, "Whatever you want." And it's not because I'm stuck between the two. It's because I genuinely do not care. I don't care if it's chicken, I don't care if it's pork, I don't care if it's a bowl of dry cereal. 

There's no struggle. I wake up, I move to the living room, and I sit. I don't debate what channel to put the TV on because I don't turn the TV on. I don't decide what shirt to wear because I just pull on whatever is sitting right there on top of the laundry basket. So, no, doctor, I'm not having any trouble making decisions. I just don't have any preference about anything in the world anymore, so there's really nothing to decide. It's all just exactly the same to me.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Do you feel your condition is worsening over time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression or worsening of the condition over time, which is not specifically covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worsening? I... I don't know if I'd say it's getting worse, exactly. It's more like... well, it's just been this same flat line for a while now. I mean, when you hit the bottom, you can't really fall any further, right? 

I think back to when this first started, maybe a couple of months ago. I was still trying to keep up appearances, you know? I'd still put on a decent shirt, maybe try to read the paper in the morning, even if none of the words were sinking in. I remember one Tuesday, I actually drove out to the hardware store to get some new sprinkler heads because a couple of ours had cracked over the winter. I walked the aisles, picked out the parts, paid the cashier. I felt completely hollow doing it, like I was just going through the motions in a play, but I was still doing it. 

But now? Now I wouldn't even think about getting in the car. I wouldn't even care if every sprinkler head in the yard was busted. But is that getting worse? Or is it just that I finally stopped pretending? I don't really know. 

It feels like I've just settled into this... this heavy, gray routine. I wake up, I sit in the chair, I watch the dust motes float in the sunlight coming through the front window, and I wait for the day to end. And the next day is exactly the same. And the day after that. There aren't any new symptoms cropping up. I'm not suddenly feeling a different kind of terrible. It's just the exact same nothingness, day in and day out. 

My wife, she keeps track of the days. She'll say, "Frank, you haven't been out of the house since last Thursday," or "Frank, you've been wearing those same sweatpants for three days." And I hear her, and I know she's right, but it doesn't feel like a progression to me. It doesn't feel like a disease that's spreading or a storm that's getting stronger. It just feels like a clock that stopped ticking. The hands are stuck at the exact same time they were stuck at yesterday, and they'll probably be stuck there tomorrow. So I really couldn't tell you if it's worsening, doctor. I just don't know how to measure it when everything is just so completely still.

patient.answer:
Restless? I... no, not at all. If anything, it's the exact opposite of that. I think I mentioned that brown leather armchair in the living room earlier, the one by the front window? Well, I can sit in that chair for... I don't even know, six, seven hours at a time, and I barely even shift my weight. 

It's actually kind of strange when I really think about it, because I used to be a guy who couldn't sit still for two minutes. Back when I was selling service contracts, I was always on the move. Always. If I was on the phone with a client, I was pacing the length of my office, back and forth, back and forth, practically wearing a track into the carpet. I'd be tapping my pen on the desk, bouncing my knee, always burning off that energy because there was always a deal to chase, always a quota to hit, always somewhere I needed to be. I was just this constant ball of motion. My wife used to tell me I made her dizzy just watching me try to watch a football game on a Sunday. 

But now... I don't have any of that. There's no pacing. There's no tapping my foot. I don't feel this urge to get up and do anything or go anywhere. I just sink into that chair. Sometimes my leg will actually fall asleep because I've been sitting in the exact same position for so long, and I won't even bother to uncross my legs to get the blood flowing again. I just let it tingle until it goes numb. It's like my body is just as heavy and quiet as my mind is these days. 

I don't feel fidgety, doctor. I don't feel anxious to get up, because there's nowhere I want to go and absolutely nothing I want to do. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm restless in the slightest. I'm just perfectly, completely still. It takes too much effort to move, and... well, there's just no point to it anyway.
